headline: High-risk filesystem and network overlap in OpenHands paired with Opik can create data leakage and cascading errors; prompt injection is lower but still plausible via shared files or APIs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write runtime files and use MCP, so if Opik ingests or relays OpenHands-produced content through a shared file or API channel, instructions can be smuggled across. Opik’s profile only shows REST API and broad egress, so the exact bridge is undocumented; uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF OpenHands writes attacker-controlled text into a file that Opik later parses as instructions
IF Opik forwards OpenHands output into a downstream prompt or agent without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of shared files by Opik
Add a provenance tag to every OpenHands-generated artifact
Require manual review before Opik consumes OpenHands output
Restrict OpenHands MCP servers to trusted endpoints only
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/ data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands explicitly touches mounted runtime files and handles model-provider API keys, while Opik has broad network egress and REST API access. If both share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive file contents can flow from OpenHands into Opik outputs or API calls. The pairwise leak path is plausible but not directly documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF OpenHands and Opik are attached to the same mounted volume or workspace
IF Opik transmits file contents or traces from that workspace to its REST API
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces
Remove secrets from any shared mounted directory
Turn off automatic upload of file contents in Opik
Rotate any API keys exposed to OpenHands
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, execute_shell, and broad network egress; Opik also has broad network egress. If they share a mutable workspace, concurrent writes or git operations can race and corrupt state. Because OpenHands supports multiple instances via mounted volume only, the shared-write pathway is explicit enough to treat as dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mounted directory
IF OpenHands and Opik modify the same git repository or files without locking
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate checkout
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Disable concurrent writes to shared paths
Use read-only mounts for Opik
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code, shell actions, and browser-driven outputs that Opik could ingest or evaluate. If Opik treats those outputs as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect evaluations or downstream actions. Opik’s profile does not show autonomous action-taking, so this is below high, but the default trust chain is still plausible.
conditions: IF Opik consumes OpenHands outputs as ground truth
IF no verification step checks OpenHands-generated facts before Opik records or forwards them
mitigations: Require a verification step before Opik accepts OpenHands output
Mark OpenHands outputs as untrusted by default
Compare outputs against source artifacts before use
Limit Opik to logging rather than acting on OpenHands results
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands handles model-provider API keys and files in a Docker runtime, while Opik is an observability/evaluation service with REST API access. No explicit residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented, so only a low compliance concern remains: if regulated files are mounted into OpenHands and then exported through Opik, policy gaps could appear. The other agent is cited because the risk is pairwise.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into OpenHands
IF Opik stores or transmits traces containing that regulated data across an external API
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Redact traces before Opik export
Use separate tenants or projects
Review retention settings in Opik
requires-engineering: document residency and DPA boundaries
